title: Passenger testifies about aftermath of fatal police shooting on Highway 401
article: A woman who was in the front passenger seat of a vehicle in a ditch on Highway 401 when the driver was shot said she saw a police officer at the open passenger window and heard a "very loud ringing."

Angela Keats, 28, Grieves' fiance, was the second Crown witness to testify Monday at the trial of OPP officer Sean O'Rourke. O'Rourke, 57, pleaded not guilty to manslaughter in the death of Nicholas Edward Grieves of Brantford.
O'Rourke also was charged with criminal negligence causing death, but that charge was withdrawn by the Crown on Monday.
Grieves, 24, was fleeing from police who were investigating the theft of $40 of gas from the Dutton ONroute rest stop on Highway 401 at about 4:30 a.m. on July 7, 2021.
Grieves was driving a 2003 Pontiac Sunfire that ended up in the ditch between the east and west lanes of the 401 near the Highgate exit.
Keats, who was in the passenger seat, testified Monday she heard an officer, whom she didn't identify, say, "Help me to get him out of the car."
Officers pulled Grieves out of the car and began trying to save his life, she said.

Keats said she had a "suspicion" the Sunfire was stolen. And when they stopped for gas that was pumped by Jonathan Wauthier, another passenger in the vehicle, she said, "I had assumed it was not paid for."
O'Rourke's defence lawyer Sandy Khehra focused on Keats's memory during his cross-examination, often comparing her testimony given in a preliminary hearing two years ago to her testimony Monday.

Having testified she and Grieves left Windsor to give Wauthier a ride to Woodstock to pick up somethings, she agreed through questions from Khehra she and Grieves were "couch surfing at the time" because of their drug use and they met Wauthier in Woodstock.
She said fentanyl was the drug of choice for both her and Grieves.
They were taking Wauthier to Windsor because he wanted to pick up an Ontario Works cheque and he would pay them some money, Keats said.
Khehra also pointed out in statements to SIU investigators Keats lied about her real name and Grieves name, that they were married, and the fact neither of them were drug users.
When questioned again by Crown attorney Jason Nicol about giving police false names, Keats said she didn't want Grieves to get into trouble.
According to the agreed statement of facts read into to court by Nicol, O'Rourke fired a single shot from his police-issued Glock Model 17 pistol, striking Grieves in the right shoulder.
The bullet hit two main arteries and despite attempts to resuscitate Grieves at the Chatham-Kent Health Alliance, he died from internal hemorrhaging of blood.
Grieves had methamphetamine and fentanyl in his system, but it was not a factor in his death, according to the post mortem report.

The agreed statement of facts also cited Grieves' past criminal record that included possession of a weapon and assault charges, which the responding officers were not aware during the encounter, Nicol told the court.
SIU forensic investigator Joseph Typer was the first witness called by the Crown.
He showed videos and photos of the Pontiac Sunfire that was being driven westbound on Highway 401 by Grieves shortly after OPP received a call at about the theft of gas.
Photos and video by the SIU also showed where an unmarked 2020 grey Dodge Durango OPP vehicle came to a stop beside the Sunfire.

Typer testified no firearms were found in the Sunfire when he examined it, but there was black folded knife under the front seat that was in the closed position. He said the knife would not have been accessible from that position.
Khehra asked Typer if he sat in the vehicle to see if he could have reached the knife.
Noting he didn't, Typer said the knife was under the driver's seat and "it could have been accessible, possibly?"
Khehra also asked Typer if he or other SIU investigators searched the area from when officers first encountered the Pontiac Sunfire to see if there were any drugs or weapons dropped.

When Typer said his focus was on where the altercation between the officer and Grieves occurred, Khehra asked if he would be surprised to hear one of the other occupants said they threw drugs out of the window.
"A drug throw would be part of the OPP investigation," Typer said.
Tricia Grieves, the mother of Nicholas Grieves, was at the courthouse in Chatham on Monday with family members as the trial began.

"It's just difficult, every day that goes by not knowing why my son was taken from me," she said. "My son, in general, he was a loving father, a great son and great grandson, he loved his grandparents very much."
O'Rourke's case is before the Superior Court of Justice. The officer has opted to be tried by judge alone rather than a jury.
Several current and retired police officers attended the trial on Monday as a show of support for O'Rourke.
The trial continues Tuesday.
